questions.question: Influx of which of the following ions contributes most to maintaining the plateau in a ventricular myocyte action potential?
questions.explanation: Inward calcium current through L-type channels helps sustain the ventricular plateau while outward potassium currents continue.
reasons: Calcium entry is the relevant inward plateau current.
Fast sodium current chiefly drives the ventricular phase-0 upstroke.
Potassium currents are primarily outward in this plateau/repolarization context, not the inward current asked for.
Chloride is not the principal inward current sustaining the plateau.

questions.question: Which of the following channels is present in Nodal cells , ventricular and purkinje.
questions.explanation: Delayed-rectifier potassium currents participate in repolarization in nodal cells as well as ventricular and Purkinje cells. Their shared role is outward potassium movement during repolarization. Other channels have more restricted or quantitatively different distributions.
reasons: The strong inward-rectifier conductance that stabilizes ventricular resting potential is not the characteristic resting conductance of SA nodal cells.
Delayed-rectifier potassium currents support repolarization in both slow-response nodal and fast-response ventricular/Purkinje tissue.
T-type calcium current contributes to pacemaking and is not the common dominant repolarizing current in all these cells.
Transient outward Ito is especially associated with the early ventricular repolarization notch, not a universal nodal-current description.

questions.question: The conduction pathway through the heart is the fastest in which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers have very rapid conduction, allowing the electrical signal to activate much of the ventricular myocardium nearly together. The AV node is deliberately slow, allowing atrial contraction and ventricular filling before ventricular activation.
reasons: Purkinje fibers conduct fastest among these listed structures and distribute excitation through the ventricles.
Bundle branches conduct rapidly, but terminal Purkinje tissue is the standard fastest-conduction answer.
The SA node is the normal pacemaker, but pacemaker dominance does not mean the fastest conduction velocity.
The His bundle carries the impulse into the ventricular conduction network but is not the fastest listed tissue.
The AV node is the slowest major conducting region and introduces a physiological delay.

questions.question: What occurs at the SA node to decrease heart rate?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine from cardiac parasympathetic fibers acts at M2 receptors. Increased potassium conductance and reduced cAMP-dependent pacemaker/calcium currents slow the SA node. The result is a longer time to threshold and a lower heart rate.
reasons: Greater inward sodium permeability during pacemaker depolarization would generally favor faster threshold attainment.
Greater calcium entry generally favors nodal excitation rather than the parasympathetic slowing described.
Reducing outward potassium conductance removes a hyperpolarizing influence and does not explain vagal slowing.
Acetylcholine activates M2 signaling, which slows SA nodal firing through potassium and cAMP-dependent mechanisms.
Norepinephrine activates beta-1 signaling and normally increases SA nodal rate.

questions.question: Which component of the ECG is the result of a conduction of a wave of depolarization through the atrial muscle?
questions.explanation: Depolarization spreads through atrial muscle and produces the P wave. Atrial contraction follows this electrical activation. The QRS and T wave describe ventricular electrical events.
reasons: The PR interval includes the P wave and atrioventricular conduction, so it is broader than atrial depolarization alone.
The P wave is the direct surface representation of atrial depolarization.
The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization.
The ST segment is associated with the ventricular plateau after activation.
The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which component of the ECG is the result of a conduction of a wave of depolarization through the atrial muscle?

questions.question: Which of the following will be a result of the direct consequences of slowing the action potential conduction to the AV node?
questions.explanation: Slower AV nodal conduction increases the time from atrial depolarization to ventricular depolarization. This prolongs the PR interval. It need not widen QRS because QRS duration reflects intraventricular conduction once ventricular activation begins.
reasons: Increased cardiac output is not a direct necessary consequence of delaying AV nodal conduction.
A widened QRS points to slower ventricular conduction, not simply an isolated AV nodal delay.
QT duration concerns ventricular depolarization and repolarization, rather than the isolated atrioventricular delay.
The PR interval includes AV nodal transit, so slowing that transit prolongs PR.

questions.question: Sympathetic nerve stimulation of AV node increases conduction velocity through the node. Which of the following is likely to decrease because of this intervention?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation increases AV nodal conduction velocity. Faster transit from atria to ventricles can shorten the PR interval. It also tends to increase heart rate and contractility, rather than reduce them.
reasons: Sympathetic stimulation usually increases rather than decreases heart rate.
Faster AV nodal conduction reduces the AV-conduction component of the PR interval.
Myocardial metabolic demand generally increases with sympathetic stimulation.
Coronary flow commonly rises to meet increased cardiac metabolic demand.
Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation generally increases cardiac contractility.

questions.question: The probability of the random desynchronization of the myocardium is highest when the electrical signal arrives at the myocardium during the vulnerable phase of the cardiac cycle. This phase corresponds with which of the following waves on the electrocardiogram (ECG)?
questions.explanation: The vulnerable period for provoking ventricular arrhythmia occurs during ventricular repolarization, around the T wave. At this time some myocardial regions may have recovered excitability while others remain refractory, permitting disorganized propagation.
reasons: The P wave is atrial depolarization and does not identify the classic ventricular vulnerable period.
The S wave is part of ventricular depolarization rather than the vulnerable repolarization phase.
The Q wave is part of the ventricular depolarization complex.
The R wave reflects ventricular depolarization, when much of the ventricle is entering refractoriness.
The T wave marks ventricular repolarization, during which heterogeneous recovery can permit dangerous re-entry.

questions.question: During which of the following phases does S3 occur?
questions.explanation: S3 occurs in early diastole during rapid ventricular filling. It is associated with vibrations as inflowing blood enters the ventricle and the ventricular wall is distended. S3 can be physiological in younger people but can indicate volume overload or systolic dysfunction in an older adult.
reasons: Rapid early ventricular filling is the phase associated with S3.
All valves are closed during isovolumetric relaxation, so rapid inflow has not yet begun.
Isovolumetric contraction occurs at the onset of systole and is associated with S1, not S3.
Slow filling occurs later in diastole than the typical S3.
Atrial contraction occurs in late diastole and is associated with S4 when the ventricle is stiff.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions decreases pulse pressure?
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure depends substantially on stroke volume and arterial compliance. Aortic stenosis can reduce and slow LV ejection, producing a small, slow-rising arterial pulse and a narrower pulse pressure. Reduced arterial compliance tends to widen pulse pressure for a given stroke volume.
reasons: Aortic stenosis can limit stroke volume and narrow pulse pressure.
Arterial stiffening with atherosclerosis tends to increase pulse pressure rather than narrow it.
An increased stroke volume tends to increase the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure.
Decreased arterial compliance tends to increase the pressure rise produced by a given stroke volume.

Semilunar opening begins ejection but does not normally generate S2.
This sequence reverses the normal ordering and incorrectly attributes a sound to opening.

questions.question: A patient at rest is given a drug that reduces the venous compliance but has no other cardiac or vascular effects. What effect will this drug have on venous return and venous blood capacity?
options: Venous return increases and venous capacity decreases
Venous return decreases and venous capacity increases
Venous return decreases and venous capacity will not change
Venous return will not change, and venous capacity will not change
Venous return will not change and venous capacity decreases
questions.explanation: Reduced venous compliance decreases the amount of blood stored at a given venous pressure. At fixed total blood volume, venoconstriction can transfer blood from unstressed to stressed volume, raise systemic filling pressure and increase the gradient for venous return.
reasons: Less venous capacitance means less storage at a given pressure and a higher driving pressure for venous return.
Increased capacity describes venodilation, the opposite of the stated compliance reduction.
A compliance reduction changes capacity; treating capacity as unchanged misses the mechanism.
The venous pressure–volume relation changes, so both capacity and the venous-return driving gradient can change.
Capacity decreases, but at fixed volume the resulting pressure rise can increase venous return rather than leave it unchanged.

questions.question: Which of the following would cause a decrease in venous return?
options: Increase in mean systemic filling pressure
Decrease in resistance to venous return
a change in right atrial pressure from 0 to -2 mmHg
questions.explanation: Reduced sympathetic venous tone allows veins to dilate and store more blood at a given pressure. This lowers stressed volume and systemic filling pressure, reducing the gradient that drives venous return. The other listed changes tend to increase that gradient or reduce resistance.
reasons: Higher systemic filling pressure increases the gradient driving blood toward the right atrium.
Lower resistance to venous return increases flow at a given pressure gradient.
Greater blood volume tends to raise filling pressure and support venous return.
Less sympathetic venoconstriction increases venous storage and can reduce the venous-return driving pressure.
Lowering right atrial pressure from 0 to −2 mmHg can increase the driving gradient before venous-collapse limitations dominate.

questions.question: After expiration of a normal tidal volume, a subject breathes in as much air as possible. Which of the following represents the volume of air inspired?
questions.explanation: At the end of a normal passive expiration, lung volume is FRC. The maximum volume that can then be inspired is inspiratory capacity, equal to tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume. It is not the entire TLC because residual and expiratory reserve volumes were already in the lungs.

questions.question: A combination of which of the following lung volumes is defined as Inspiratory Capacity?
options: Inspiratory Reserve Volume + Tidal Volume + Expiratory reserve volume
Residual Volume + Expiratory Reserve Volume +Tidal Volume + Inspiratory Reserve Volume
questions.explanation: Inspiratory capacity is the maximum volume inspired from the end of a normal expiration. It therefore includes a normal tidal inspiration plus the additional inspiratory reserve volume. Residual and expiratory reserve volumes are not newly inspired in this maneuver.
reasons: Adding ERV gives vital capacity, not inspiratory capacity.
Adding every listed volume gives total lung capacity, including residual volume.
ERV plus RV equals functional residual capacity.
ERV plus tidal volume omits IRV and includes an expiratory component.
Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume is inspiratory capacity.

questions.question: What is the effect of increasing surface tension?
options: It is absent at the air-liquid interface

reasons: Higher surface tension opposes inflation rather than facilitating it.
Surface tension increases, not minimizes, the tendency of alveoli to collapse.
Unopposed surface tension can destabilize smaller alveoli rather than provide the stabilizing effect of surfactant.
Greater inward recoil means less volume change for a given pressure change, reducing compliance.
Surface tension is generated at the air–liquid interface rather than being absent there.

SAQ 1) An 80-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after
fainting during a church service. Her ECG trace in the emergency department is shown in the
accompanying image. Which of the following answer choices best describes the irregularity noted on this
patient's ECG?
A) Atrial fibrillation
B) Premature atrial complexes
C) Second-degree heart block type I
D) Second-degree heart block type II
E) Third-degree heart block
questions.sourceExplanation: C

questions.question: SAQ 2) What are points A and B representing?
questions.printedAnswer:
A: Bradycardia on expiration
B: Tachycardia on inspiration
questions.sourceExplanation:
A: Bradycardia on expiration
B: Tachycardia on inspiration

SAQ 3) Dixon, a 63-year-old man presented to the ER with progressive shortness of breath for the last
five years. He fatigues easily and has lost all his energy to do anything. He also complains of anorexia.
Last night he awoke suddenly from sleep because of shortness of breath and developed a dry cough. The
breathing problem improved when he sat on the edge of his bed for an hour. Previously, he had
myocardial infarction, mitral stenosis and hypertension. He generally sleeps with two, sometimes three
pillows. He has not experienced chest pain, leg pain or fainting spells. His CXR showed enlarged heart
with pulmonary congestion. He is taking Digitalis (cardiac glycoside, an inotropic agent) and Furosemide
tablets (diuretic) for his ongoing condition.
1. What is your diagnosis?
questions.sourceExplanation: Decompensated heart failure

1. What is your diagnosis?
questions.sourceExplanation: Pulmonary edema

questions.question: 4. How does Digitalis (as an inotropic agent) work?
questions.printedAnswer:
Digitalis bonds to ATPase (Na-K pump) and inhibits it, thus sodium is retained inside the
cardiomyocytes and do not leave the cell. This affects the Na-Ca exchanger that normally brings sodium and let
calcium out. Due to the high concentration of sodium inside, morecalcium accumulates inside the cell
improving heart contractility

SAQ 5) During normal spontaneous breathing, the respiratory parameters of a healthy 25-year-old male
are measured as: Tidal volume (VT) =500 ml and Respiratory frequency (FR) =16 breaths/min.
Following a thorax injury, breathing becomes very painful for this individual. To reduce the magnitude
of chest movement by breathing and reduce pain, the physician decides to ventilate him artificially (using
a ventilator) with a smaller tidal volume but with a higher frequency than his spontaneous breathing. His
VT is set to 250 ml and FR to 32 breaths/min. (Repeated)
1. What is Total ventilation, Alveolar ventilation, and Dead space Ventilation of this person before and
after artificial ventilation?
questions.printedAnswer:
Before artificial ventilation:
- Total ventilation: 500 × 16 = 8000 mL
- Alveolar ventilation: 350 × 16 = 5600 mL
- Dead ventilation: 150 × 16 = 2400 mL
After artificial ventilation:
- Total ventilation: 250 × 32 = 8000 mL
- Alveolar ventilation: 100 × 32 = 3200 mL
- Dead ventilation: 150 × 32 = 4800 mL
questions.sourceExplanation:
Before artificial ventilation:
- Total ventilation: 500 × 16 = 8000 mL
- Alveolar ventilation: 350 × 16 = 5600 mL
- Dead ventilation: 150 × 16 = 2400 mL
After artificial ventilation:
- Total ventilation: 250 × 32 = 8000 mL
- Alveolar ventilation: 100 × 32 = 3200 mL
- Dead ventilation: 150 × 32 = 4800 mL

questions.question: 2. What change in arterial PO2 will occur after the transition to artificial ventilation?
questions.printedAnswer: PO2 will decrease because of decreased alveolar ventilation.

questions.question:
SAQ 7) A man traveled to a high-altitude location where the barometric pressure was 580 mmHg,
compared to the normal 760 mmHg at sea level.
Q1) How does the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PᵢO₂) change at this altitude compared to sea
level?
questions.printedAnswer:
At higher altitudes, the barometric pressure decreases, leading to a reduction in the
partial pressure of inspired oxygen.
questions.sourceExplanation:
At higher altitudes, the barometric pressure decreases, leading to a reduction in the
partial pressure of inspired oxygen.

questions.question: Q2) What effect does this altitude have on alveolar ventilation?
questions.printedAnswer:
Alveolar ventilation increases at high altitudes due to hypoxemia, which stimulates the peripheral
chemoreceptors. These receptors signal the respiratory center to increase the rate and depth of breathing
(hyperventilation) to improve oxygen uptake.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 7) A man traveled to a high-altitude location where the barometric pressure was 580 mmHg,
compared to the normal 760 mmHg at sea level.
Q1) How does the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PᵢO₂) change at this altitude compared to sea
level?
questions.sourceExplanation:
Alveolar ventilation increases at high altitudes due to hypoxemia, which stimulates the peripheral
chemoreceptors. These receptors signal the respiratory center to increase the rate and depth of breathing
(hyperventilation) to improve oxygen uptake.

questions.question: Q3) How does the activity of peripheral chemoreceptors respond to this change in altitude?
questions.printedAnswer:
Peripheral chemoreceptors become more active in response to the reduced partial
pressure of oxygen in arterial blood (PaO₂). They detect hypoxemia and stimulate the respiratory center to
increase ventilation. This response helps mitigate the effects of low oxygen availability at high altitudes.

SAQ 35) A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a two-week history of
progressive fatigue, severe dizziness, and two recent episodes of near fainting (presyncope).
On examinations, his blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, and his pulse is regular at 36 beats per
minute. A 12-lead ECG shows complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes,
with an atrial rate of 80 bpm and a ventricular escape rate of 36 bpm. He is diagnosed with
third-degree (complete) atrioventricular (AV) block and admitted to the cardiac care unit for
urgent temporary pacing.
Q1: Explain the concept of an "escape rhythm" in the context of a complete AV block and
describe how the intrinsic firing rates change as you move down the cardiac conduction
system.
questions.printedAnswer:
Escape rhythm acts like a backup in case of pacemaker (SA node) failure,
SA node: 60–100 beats/min
AV node: 40–60 beats/min
Bundle of His/Purkinje fibers: 20–40 beats/min

SAQ 36) A 62-year-old male with a long-standing history of untreated essential hypertension
presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset, worsening
shortness of breath and a persistent cough producing pink, frothy sputum.
On physical examination, his blood pressure is 210/120 mmHg, his heart rate is 105
bpm, and bilateral pulmonary rates are heard halfway up both lung fields (indicating
pulmonary edema). An echocardiogram reveals signs of severely elevated ventricular
filling pressures with an overall reduced ejection fraction, but notable stiffening of the
left ventricular wall without any documented signs of permanent tissue remodeling.
Shortly after admission, he develops crushing retrosternal pain radiating to the inner
(medial) left arm. ECG and coronary angiography show ischemia of the anterior wall of
the left ventricle and the apex.
Q1. Describe how the patient's acute hypertensive crisis alters the appearance of his PV
loop (red dashed lines) compared to a healthy individual (green continuous line). Which
change (increased, decreased & no change) will be expected in the following
parameters?
A. End-Systolic Volume (ESV)
B. Stroke Volume (SV)
C. Peak Systolic Pressure
questions.printedAnswer:
ESV is increased, Stroke volume is decreased, and Peak systolic Pressure is
increased
questions.sourceExplanation:
ESV is increased, Stroke volume is decreased, and Peak systolic Pressure is
increased

questions.printedAnswer:
A) Because they have narrow lumens and smooth muscle walls, producing high
resistance to blood flow.
B) Their smooth muscles adjust to lumen through active vasoconstriction and
vasodilation

The referred pain to the medial side of the arm occurs due to the shared nerve pathways

The heart and the medial side of the arm are both innervated by spinal segments T1-T4, leading to
referred pain during myocardial infarction.

questions.question:
A) list down the contents of the middle mediastinum:
B) list down the contents of the posterior mediastinum:
C) name the structure covered in red and state its function:
questions.printedAnswer:
A)
● Heart within the pericardium
● Roots of great vessels ( aorta, pulmonary arteries and veins, SVC, IVC)
● Phrenic nerve
● Main bronchi
● Arch of the azygous vein
B)
● Esophagus (with vagal plexuses)
● Descending aorta and branches
● Azygos and Hemiazygos venous systems
● Thoracic duct
● Sympathetic trunk and splanchnic nerves
C) Phrenic nerve function: The phrenic nerves provide motor innervation to the diaphragm and work in
conjunction with secondary respirator muscles (trapezius, pectoralis major, pectoralis minor,
sternocleidomastoid, and intercostals) to allow respiration.
questions.sourceExplanation:
A)
● Heart within the pericardium

● Arch of the azygous vein
B)
● Esophagus (with vagal plexuses)
● Descending aorta and branches
● Azygos and Hemiazygos venous systems
● Thoracic duct
● Sympathetic trunk and splanchnic nerves
C) Phrenic nerve function: The phrenic nerves provide motor innervation to the diaphragm and work in
conjunction with secondary respirator muscles (trapezius, pectoralis major, pectoralis minor,
